source_document.body:
There will be a little more than 2,400 new truck parking spaces built over the next few years as a result of funding provided to various projects under the Nationally Significant Multimodal Freight & Highway Projects (INFRA) program.
“A targeted objective of this funding opportunity is to directly address the national shortage of commercial motor vehicle parking,” the Department of Transportation said in announcing the grants Wednesday. “By funding projects that expand safe, accessible public parking for commercial drivers, the Department aims to reduce fatigue-related accidents, improve supply chain fluidity, and provide essential infrastructure along the nation’s most critical freight corridors. To support these national freight and mobility goals, the Department intends to invest in projects that enhance or maintain the operational efficiency of the national transportation network.”
According to an FAQ document on INFRA, the funds for parking can only be provided to some sort of public entity or a public-private partnership. The list of acceptable entities to apply included potential applicants as big as a state or a group of them, down to an individual local government or a group of them.
But it also provides that any of the public applicants could have applied with a “private entity to fund development, capacity expansion, or operations and maintenance.”
There were 14 new parking projects approved by INFRA and announced by the Department of Transportation Wednesday. The precise total of new spots is 2,403.
Biggest project in the Volunteer State
The largest is a 500 spot project in Tennessee. That project is actually two separate projects, one near Nashville and the other near Knoxville.
The recipients of the grant of just under $24 million are three counties, joined together under the banner of the Greater Nashville Regional Council. The new parking spots will be built at five separate Pilot Travel Center locations, according to the fact sheet released by the DOT. They will be built along interstate 40 and interstate 24.
Border crossing parking
The dropoff to the next largest project is significant: 305 spots to be built in Los Indios, Texas, near the Brownsville border crossing with Mexico.
In that project, according to the DOT, work will need to be done to reconstruct about 0.35 miles of a local road that will provide access to a new parking area near the Los Indios Port of Entry. Cameron County was the entity granted the $9.2 million award.
The other projects from largest to smallest, along with their sponsors, are as follows:
Port of Savannah, 275 spots, sponsored by the Georgia Ports Authority, near the port of Savannah, less than two miles from gate 4 of the port, $24.5 million.
Enfield, Connecticut, 260 spots at a new parking facility, sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation, on interstate 91 north of Hartford, $13.5 million.
Rest Iowa sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation, described as “rural,” 150 spots spread out over six existing rest areas on interstate 80, $24.5 million, sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation.
Port of Wilmington, North Carolina, 140 spots, $6 million, at the port, serving interstate 40, sponsored by the North Carolina State Ports Authority.
Interstate 49 rest area, new project on the future interstate 49 in Crawford County, Arkansas, 137 spots, $23 million, Arkansas Department of Transportation is the sponsor.
Nebraska interstate 80 rest stop, sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation, 120 spots for $7.5 million, building a new facility between mile markers 247 and 254 in Dawson County.
Monroe County, Georgia, 109 spots, $13.5 million, adding spots at existing sites at two Georgia-owned parking facilities, one a weigh station and one a rest area, sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation.
Wisconsin project on interstate 41 near Dodge County, sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation, 106 spots for $15 million, adding to two existing areas.
Fort Worth Alliance project at a Pilot Travel Center, 100 spots, $5 million, state highway 170 & interstate 35 west, sponsored by the city of Fort Worth.
Needles truck parking area, 100 spots at a new 15-acre site, near the interstate 40 and California 95 interchange, $6.4 million, sponsored by the city of Needles.
Fergus Falls rest area in Minnesota, 63 spots, $27.7 million, sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation, located on interstate 94.
Southern Illinois project, sponsored by the state’s Department of Transportation, 38 parking spots, reconstructing the southbound Green Creek and Post Oak rest areas on interstate 57.

source_document.body:
Proposed reliability standards that would require qualifying data centers, artificial intelligence facilities, and cryptocurrency operations to provide grid data, coordinate protection settings, and respond to grid operators’ instructions have passed their final stakeholder ballot, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) announced Oct. 15 .
The standards and associated implementation plans will next go before NERC’s Board of Trustees for adoption, followed by submission to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) for U.S. regulatory approval, the organization said in its announcement.
The Project 2026-02 package includes three new computational-load standards and revisions to two existing facility-interconnection standards. The new standards would apply to computational-load sites with at least 50 MW of total connected load supplied through electrical equipment connected at 100 kV or above, from one or more points of connection, under the final-ballot applicability provisions .
The vote advances the technical requirements behind FERC’s July 16 directive , which required NERC to file initial computational-load standards by Dec. 31, 2026. A separate registration effort also progressed on Oct. 8, when NERC’s board approved proposed Rules of Procedure revisions to establish Computational Load Owner and Computational Load Operator as two functional entity types, according to NERC’s third-quarter Large Loads Action Plan update .
Which Data Centers Would Be Subject to NERC’s Reliability Standards?
The proposed framework distinguishes the entity that owns and maintains a computational-load site from the entity that operates it, according to the final glossary definitions . Individual registration determinations would depend on each entity’s circumstances and would be conducted through NERC and the relevant Regional Entities, NERC’s October project FAQ says.
The 100-kV criterion concerns the electrical equipment supplying the site, typically its high-side voltage, rather than necessarily the point of connection identified in an interconnection agreement, the FAQ explains . The requirements would cover existing and future qualifying sites, and applicable utilities, planners, and grid operators would have duties alongside computational-load owners and operators, the document states.
The threshold is narrower than NERC’s initial registration proposal: the minimum load and voltage criteria increased from 20 MW and 60 kV to 50 MW and 100 kV following stakeholder comments, according to the third-quarter update . The board also authorized expedited development of a data request to support registration of computational-load owners and operators, pending FERC approval of the proposed registry criteria, the update says.
Proposed NERC Standards Cover Data Center Modeling, Operations, and Protection
The first new standard, CLO-001-1 , would require coordinated interconnection studies, commissioning procedures, and planning-model data for computational-load sites. Transmission planners and planning coordinators would study new connections and existing sites seeking a “qualified change,” and planning coordinators would maintain a publicly available definition of that term under the proposed standard.
The required modeling information would include settings and capabilities related to tripping, ride-through, and recovery after disturbances, as well as the amount and expected use of information-technology infrastructure, under CLO-001-1 . Owners would provide model-verification documentation to show that configurable, site-specific parameters represent installed equipment, including updates within 180 days after hardware, software, firmware, or setting changes that alter dynamic response, the standard specifies.
The second standard, CLO-002-1 , would establish operational-data and communications obligations. Transmission operators, balancing authorities, and reliability coordinators would document their data needs, and computational-load owners and operators that receive those specifications would have to satisfy them under the proposal.
Among its most consequential provisions, computational-load operators would have to comply with operating instructions from their transmission operator, balancing authority, or reliability coordinator unless the action could not be physically implemented or would violate safety, equipment, regulatory, or statutory requirements, under Requirement R8 . Operators unable to comply would have to notify the issuing entity, and personnel who receive oral operating instructions would need initial training in confirming or requesting repetition of those instructions, the standard states.
The third standard, CLO-003-1 , addresses protection coordination and disturbance monitoring, including breaker-status records, fault recordings, and continuous dynamic disturbance data. Load owners would also establish and use a process for developing protection settings so protective systems operate in the intended sequence during faults, including resolving identified coordination issues before implementation, under its requirements.
Recording responsibilities would depend partly on equipment ownership: where a utility or generator owner owns the main transformer supplying the site, that entity would bear the applicable fault- and dynamic-disturbance-recording duties, according to the CLO-003-1 implementation plan . Changes to existing standards FAC-001 and FAC-002 are intended to avoid duplicative interconnection requirements, according to the associated implementation plan .
Data Center Industry Questions Multitenant Compliance Responsibilities
How those obligations would work at multitenant facilities was a substantive issue during development: a site operator may lack authority over tenants’ equipment, access to their information, or the technical ability to change their consumption, the Data Center Coalition argued in comments summarized in the drafting team’s response document . Data requests should not require owners and operators to provide information outside their control or access, the coalition said in those comments.
A dedicated on-site operating organization is not required, and a centralized or shared function could serve as the accountable operator, the drafting team said in responses to Meta and the coalition . Allocation of responsibility at multitenant sites would depend on registration and operational responsibilities, and NERC staff were developing additional registration clarity, the team said in the same document.
The existing exceptions for physically infeasible actions and safety, equipment, regulatory, or statutory restrictions provide limits on operating instructions, the drafting team said in its responses . The final text retains those exceptions rather than expressly adding the contractual and third-party-control exclusions sought by the coalition, as reflected in CLO-002-1 .
Proposed NERC Compliance Timelines Extend Up to Three Years After Standards Take Effect
The year-end FERC filing deadline is not a deadline for facilities to comply: the proposed plans establish effective dates tied to regulatory approval and then allow additional implementation periods, as set out in the CLO-001-1 plan . In jurisdictions requiring approval, that standard would become effective on the first day of the first calendar quarter after the approving order’s effective date, unless the relevant authority provides otherwise, the plan specifies.
Planning coordinators would have three months after CLO-001-1’s effective date to establish qualified-change definitions, and planning coordinators and transmission planners would jointly develop modeling-data requirements within the same period, under its phased schedule . Interconnection-requirement duties would follow at six months, and the remaining study and owner-data obligations at nine months, under the same schedule . For operational data and communications, grid entities would have six months to establish and distribute data specifications, while owners and operators would generally have 12 months for data provision, operating-instruction, communications, and training obligations under the CLO-002-1 plan .
Disturbance monitoring has the longest proposed transition: sites in service on or before CLO-003-1’s effective date would have 36 months to meet its recording requirements, under the implementation plan . Sites entering service afterward would have until 15 months after the standard’s effective date or their in-service date, whichever is later; protection-coordination duties would begin after nine months, the plan specifies.
The monitoring schedule accounts for equipment procurement, installation, and necessary outages, according to the plan . For sites in service no later than 12 months after the standard’s effective date, entities could request extensions of the monitoring requirements if circumstances beyond their control prevent equipment installation, under the implementation plan . Those periods remain proposed, and the standards still require board adoption and applicable regulatory approval, NERC said in its Oct. 15 announcement .
Minimum Voltage and Frequency Ride-Through Standards Remain Under Development
The package responds to gaps identified through NERC’s incident reviews, Large Loads Working Group, and May Level 3 Essential Action Alert , which addressed modeling, studies, commissioning, protection, monitoring, and operational coordination for computational loads. The alert called for assessment of aggregate load reductions, including customer-initiated reductions, that could cause planning-criteria violations, as well as better information about facilities’ protection and control responses.
However, this initial package does not establish industry-wide minimum voltage and frequency ride-through performance requirements—the conditions under which facilities must continue operating through electrical disturbances—as NERC explicitly states in its October FAQ . Its interconnection provisions can accommodate ride-through criteria based on grid-performance needs, but broader minimum performance requirements are a separate development effort, the document explains.
Additional work is proceeding on disturbance performance, computational-load-loss studies, and event reporting and model validation, according to the third-quarter action-plan update . A work plan for subsequent computational-load standards is due to FERC by March 1, 2027, under the July order .

KYIV, Ukraine — The U.S. appears to have stopped sharing some forms of key intelligence with Kyiv, Ukrainian officials said Wednesday, dealing a blow to the country’s capacity to defend its skies and to continue its highly effective mid- and long-range strike campaign.
U.S. President Donald Trump has so far denied that there had been any interruption in Starlink connectivity or incoming missile warnings — the two forms of American intelligence that Ukrainian officials say are no longer flowing freely to Kyiv.
The crisis comes just days after Trump told allies that the U.S. would ease sanctions on Russian diesel last week during peace talks in Miami. He then reportedly threatened to cut off intelligence and weapons sales to Kyiv if it kept striking Russia’s oil infrastructure, according to CNN .
“Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American President announced a ceasefire in the energy sector. But Russia did not listen,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
“Unfortunately, there was a ballistic missile strike on Kyiv yesterday, and there was no warning from our partners regarding this attack. Usually, such a warning is provided, and it is a crucial factor that aids our defense.”
Partner intelligence is an indispensable asset for Kyiv, which relies on NATO and especially U.S. information for both offensive and defensive operations. Curtailing that relationship could cost civilian lives along with the virtual stalemate Ukraine has managed to establish along the frontline, according to Ukrainian officials.
“Intelligence data on the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save people’s lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is what helps prevent people being killed when there is a warning about ballistics,” Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
On Sunday, Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow — without the confirmation of either party, officials from both countries said.
Ukraine initially resisted Trump’s push to spare Russia’s oil network, repeating that it would stop hitting refineries only if Moscow stopped striking Ukrainian power plants. After Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” that Moscow never accepted, Kyiv held its fire for three days. Russia, however, did not.
Kyiv residents heard at least five powerful explosions Sunday night before air-raid sirens sounded.
Rumors immediately circulated that the missing alert stemmed from a disruption in partner intelligence, but officials initially urged people not to jump to conclusions.
“You can call me an optimist, but I don’t believe (I don’t want to believe) that the United States will leave us without this information,” presidential adviser and communications expert Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov wrote Monday on Telegram , noting that Ukraine still relies on partners for reports of ballistic missile launches.
“Because it’s about the survival of civilians,” he wrote.
But when more missiles and drones struck Kyiv the following day, mainly targeting energy infrastructure and the power grid, reports began surfacing across the country that strike drones, interceptors and frontline vehicles were losing connection above roughly 100 mph (160 km/h), units across the country reported.
By Wednesday, multiple officials confirmed that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted Starshield, the military version of its Starlink service, without notice, just as Kyiv struggles against faster Russian jet drones , larger ballistic and cruise missile barrages and a global shortage of missile interceptors .
“This complicates UAV missions, particularly those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones, and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay,” the Ministry of Defense said in a statement on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy ended the pause on hitting Russian energy facilities on Wednesday after Kremlin forces kept striking Ukraine’s grid days after Trump declared a ceasefire.
“We’re done,” he told the Financial Times after making the decision.

Katie Livingstone is the Ukraine correspondent for Defense News and Military Times. Based in Kyiv, she has covered Russia's full-scale invasion since its first days. She is a former Fulbright fellow whose award-winning work has appeared in outlets across Europe and the U.S.

Europe’s EV sales just posted a record September, as global market growth shifts toward Europe and beyond its largest established markets.
Almost 600,000 EVs were sold in Europe in September, up 39% year over year, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence . Globally, sales reached 2.15 million, up 17% from August but down 2% from September 2025.
Region | Sept-26, million | y-o-y | m-o-m | YTD, millions | YTD-26 vs YTD-25
China | 1.11 | -18% | 7% | 8.1 | -13%
Europe | 0.60 | 39% | 62% | 3.9 | 30%
North America | 0.13 | -44% | -8% | 1.2 | -24%
RoW | 0.31 | 81% | 6% | 2.3 | 93%
Global | 2.15 | -2% | 17% | 15.5 | 3%
That brings worldwide sales of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) to 15.5 million through September, up 3% from the same period last year. But where those EVs are selling tells a much more interesting story.
Europe hits a new EV sales record
Europe’s September total beat its previous record, set in June, by 10%. BEVs did most of the heavy lifting: Their sales jumped 50% year over year, compared with 16% growth for PHEVs.

The UK, France, Spain, Portugal, and Finland all posted their highest monthly EV sales ever. France’s sales climbed 78% year over year to almost 80,000, while Germany’s rose 61% to 117,000.
UK sales were more than 3.5 times August’s total, although there’s an important point to take into account: September’s new registration plates give the entire British car market a seasonal boost. EVs’ share of UK sales stayed roughly flat from August at around 40%.
Across Europe, EV sales rose 62% month over month as buyers returned after the summer slowdown. Through September, the region has sold 3.9 million EVs, up 30% year over year.
North America’s 44% drop needs some context
North America went the opposite direction. September EV sales fell 44% year over year to around 130,000 – the region’s steepest percentage decline of 2026. Sales also slipped 8% from August.
But that headline number comes with a big caveat. September 2025 was the final month before the US federal $7,500 EV tax credit expired, so buyers rushed to buy EVs before the deadline. This September is being measured against that huge sales month.
That doesn’t erase the region’s struggles, though. North American EV sales totaled 1.2 million through September, down 24% from a year earlier. But Benchmark cautions against reading the September percentage as a sudden new collapse in demand.
“From the fourth quarter, the comparison will be against the months immediately after the credit’s removal, when US EV sales collapsed, so the year-on-year picture should improve markedly,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.
In other words, smaller declines later this year won’t necessarily mean sales have recovered – the comparison will just be less stark.
China’s automakers look overseas
China is still by far the largest EV market, with 1.11 million sold in September. That’s up 7% from August, but down 18% year over year, a deeper decline than August’s 11% drop.
Through September, China’s EV sales totaled 8.1 million, down 13%. PHEVs account for much of that weakness: Their sales are down 25% this year, compared with a 6% decline for BEVs.
Chinese gas car sales are down 43% year-on-year to 534,000 units in September 2026, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) . So falling EV sales don’t mean drivers are buying gas cars.
Chinese automakers have kept production steady and sent more vehicles abroad. Passenger car exports in China’s new energy vehicle category reached a monthly record of 558,000 in September.
But two policy changes could make that export strategy tougher next year. An EU–China agreement, still subject to member-state approval, would cap imports of Chinese-built BEVs and PHEVs at 350,000 in 2027. The four-year arrangement would raise the cap by 6% annually after its first year.
China will also cut its export VAT rebate for new energy vehicles from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, reducing the tax refund available to exporters.
The rest of the world keeps growing
Outside China, Europe, and North America, September EV sales rose 81% year over year to around 310,000.

On the heels of an experimentation ramp-up that has seen the U.S. Army’s high-altitude balloons deployed to Europe, the Pacific and the Middle East, a missile defense official said Wednesday that all options were on the table as the service seeks to make the most of the capability.
Col. Joseph Mroszczyk , director of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command’s Transformation Integration Directorate – Space Superiority (TID-SS), said in a briefing with reporters Wednesday at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting that he was pushing for “a family of stratospheric systems” that included high-altitude balloons of all sizes.
“What that enables us to do is provide space-like capabilities, really exploiting a transition point between what is normally considered the aerial layer and the space domain,” Mroszczyk said.
“That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from the stratosphere … being able to go and take advantage of winds that are pushing you where you want to go already, to be able to get either launched effects or other types of payloads for sensing and communication and extension of your launched effects portfolio.”
While using balloons as shooters, as Ukraine has reportedly done , likely presents a bigger set of challenges than using them for sensing, Mroszczyk said nothing was off the table.
“I wouldn’t say that we’re going to hold back from opportunities and options that would include something that could be kinetic in nature,” he said. “But right now, we’re doing experiments across the board with all types of different payloads.”
The stratosphere is the layer of Earth’s atmosphere above the lowest layer, the troposphere. The Army uses the term to refer to the stretch from about 60,000 to 100,000 feet, or 11 to 19 miles above Earth. On Wednesday, Mroszczyk invoked the term “ space littorals ” to describe the band, referencing the Navy’s language for the shallow waters nearest the coast.
High-altitude balloons are not a new military concept. Famously, a Chinese balloon drifted into U.S. airspace in 2023, raising national security alarms and leading to the discovery of several previous incursions that had gone undetected.
A high-altitude Chinese surveillance balloon floats over Billings, Montana, on Feb. 1, 2023. (Larry Mayer/The Billings Gazette via AP)
A 2019 Army University Press article extolled the potential of military balloons as space operations came to the forefront.
“Intuitively, balloons at such heights could perform missions such as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, communications, missile warning, and precision navigation and timing,” Lt. Col. Anthony Tingle wrote . “As the space domain becomes increasingly precarious, balloons offer resilience and redundancy against overhead capability shortfalls.”
The Army’s current interest in the balloons and their potential is unprecedented, though.
In the briefing on Wednesday, the commander of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, said the systems had been deployed for testing and demonstration to Europe, the Pacific and Morocco.
Breaking Defense reported further about the balloons’ presence in the Middle East this week, citing officials who said small swarms of a few dozen drones were deployed in the region for testing after a plan to do a much larger demonstration in the Pacific was scrapped.
The commander of the Army’s 3rd Multi-Domain Task Force, Col. Wade Germann, told Military Times earlier this week that his unit was actively developing new operating concepts for the balloons.
“We work them in a format called constellation approach, where we’ll put a couple of the high, high-end, really exclusive ones up there with different payloads and systems on them,” Germann said. “And then we’ll work in a different venue where we’ll look at cheap, very expendable, rapidly employable, in that you can put up hundreds at a time and create multiple dilemmas for the enemy on.”
Germann said the Army was working with industry to develop the most useful capabilities and determine not only the right payloads, but the right lifting gas and launch methodology.
“That’s the way that we’re working with our partners out in the field to gain that real-time feedback and make these things happen,” he said.
Over the course of the coming year, Mroszczyk said, the Army planned to conduct multiple balloon experiments aimed at determining the best ways to “exploit the stratosphere.”
Rafferty said seeing the balloons in action had turned him into a “huge believer” in their potential.
“Every time they are demonstrated in the Pacific or in Europe, there are more and more; they gain more and more support,” he said. “So we’re, I think, really excited about this next year, about what we’re going to do to further the program.”

2027 Kia Sorento HEV Drops With a $39,090 Price Tag, Undercuts Honda Pilot
10 photos
Photo: Kia
Kia has just revealed pricing for its new 2027 Sorento HEV, and the configurator went live with new tech features and optional blackout exterior elements for the one below it. Kia’s mid-size SUV undercuts the Honda Pilot and Mazda CX-90, but arrives more expensive than its brother from another mother, the Hyundai Santa Fe.
The 2027 Kia Sorento HEV arrives in America with a starting price of $39,090. For the money, customers get the base trim, the Sorento HEV EX with front-wheel drive. Those who want to go home with a Sorento HEV X-Line EX with all-wheel drive will pay $1,800 more.
Regardless of the traction wheels, the base trim gets an eight-way power-adjustable driver’s seat, heated front seats, the 12.3-inch touchscreen with navigation, a six-speaker audio system, the seven-seat layout, and the Smart Power Liftgate.
Upper in the range sits the Kia Sorento HEV X-Line EX, which is a $43,090 deal. This version is available with all-wheel drive only. For the money, buyers get the new blackout exterior design elements, along with matching gloss-black wheels and premium machined wood inlays inside the cabin.
Photo: Kia A panoramic sunroof, the SynTex seat upholstery, and second-row Captain's Chairs are also on board Kia’s all-new midsize SUV, while the Bose Premium Audio provides the soundtrack inside the cabin.
The Sorento HEV X-Line SX-Prestige sits at the top of the lineup, expectedly with the highest price: it starts at $47,590. The range-topping version comes with the 360-degree Surround View Monitor and Navigation-Based Smart Cruise Control with Stop & Go.
The driver gets a 14-way power seat with memory, four-way power lumbar adjustment, and two-way power thigh extension, along with aluminum sport pedals. Leather upholstery and a heated second row are also on board. The range-topping SX-Prestige also gains a standard Head-Up Display, while it is not available on the lower EX or X-Line EX trims.
The "HEV" lettering shows up on the tailgate, while the Sorento lineup ditches the old Steel Gray exterior paint in favor of the new Pale Gray, which can be selected at no extra cost. In the meantime, the Premium Paint options cost $495.
Photo: Kia Regardless of the trim, the 2027 Kia Sorento HEV retains the already familiar setup, which integrates the 1.6-liter inline-four turbocharged gas engine with direct injection, paired with a permanent magnet synchronous electric motor. Together, they produce 227 horsepower (230 metric horsepower) and 258 pound-feet (350 Newton meters) of torque.
The front-wheel-drive entry-level variant does 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 7.2 seconds. Because they are heavier, the all-wheel-drive variants need roughly half a second more, which is still impressive for the midsize SUV segment. Top speed is electronically limited at 120 mph (193 kph).
Kia also offers a cheaper and a more expensive Sorento in the United States. The base Sorento comes with a 2.5-liter, zero electrification, and 191 horsepower (194 metric horsepower) for a starting price of $32,590.
In the meantime, the Sorento Plug-in Hybrid with the 1.6-liter turbocharged inline-four and an electric motor for 261 horsepower (268 metric horsepower) will set you back $48,290.

The cell is the fundamental unit of life, forming the building block of all living organisms. Cells carry out essential functions such as energy conversion, reproduction, and communication. The study of cells—cell biology—is central to understanding biology, medicine, and biotechnology.
Key Points About Cells
A cell is the smallest unit of life that can carry out all life processes.
All living organisms consist of one or more cells.
Cells can exist independently (unicellular) or as part of multicellular organisms.
Two main types of cells exist: prokaryotic (without a nucleus ) and eukaryotic (with a nucleus).
Cells contain specialized structures ( organelles , in eukaryotic cells) that perform distinct functions.
Cells reproduce through division, either asexually ( mitosis or binary fission) or sexually ( meiosis ).
The cell theory is a fundamental principle in biology explaining the properties and significance of cells.
Download and Print the Cell Diagram and Glossary
For classroom use, studying, or quick reference, download and print these helpful cell biology resources:
Cell Definition and Diagram ( PDF ): Includes labeled diagrams of prokaryotic, plant, and animal cells, plus a clear one-sentence definition of a cell.
Cell Biology Glossary ( PDF ): A printable glossary of essential cell terms, alphabetized and designed to fit on a single page in 12 pt Cantarell font.
To download: Right-click the image (PNG) or PDF link and select “Save as…” or tap and hold on mobile. You may print as many copies as you need for personal or educational use.
What Is a Cell?
Definition : A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of an organism, typically microscopic, consisting of cytoplasm and a membrane, and in most cases containing a nucleus and organelles.
What a Cell Is :
A bacterium (e.g., Escherichia coli )
A skin cell from a human (epithelial cell)
A neuron (nerve cell)
A paramecium (a unicellular protist)
What a Cell Is Not :
A virus (not considered alive or cellular; lacks metabolism and independent reproduction)
DNA alone (a molecule, not a living unit)
A mitochondrion (a cell organelle, not a cell)
A water droplet or crystal (not alive and not composed of cells)
Characteristics of Cells
All cells share the following characteristics:
Surrounded by a plasma membrane
Contain cytoplasm
Possess genetic material ( DNA or RNA )
Have ribosomes for protein synthesis
Capable of metabolism and homeostasis
Can reproduce (by division)
Respond to environmental stimuli
Types of Cells
There are two main types of cells:
Prokaryotic Cells No true nucleus (DNA floats in the cytoplasm) Lack membrane-bound organelles Found in bacteria and archaea
Eukaryotic Cells Contain a membrane-bound nucleus Possess various organelles (e.g., mitochondria, Golgi apparatus ) Found in animals, plants, fungi , and protists
Comparison of Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
Feature | Prokaryotic Cells | Eukaryotic Cells
Nucleus | No (nucleoid region) | Yes (membrane-bound nucleus)
Size | Small (0.1–5 µm) | Larger (10–100 µm)
Organelles | No membrane-bound organelles | Many membrane-bound organelles
DNA | Circular, in cytoplasm | Linear, inside the nucleus
Cell Division | Binary fission | Mitosis or meiosis
Examples | Bacteria, Archaea | Animals, plants, fungi, protists
Cellular Structure
Cells consist of a variety of internal and external structures that perform specialized functions necessary for survival and reproduction. These components vary depending on whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic, and whether it belongs to a plant, animal, fungus, or protist. Understanding each part’s structure, location, and function helps explain how cells operate as self-contained units of life.
Structure | Description | Location | Function | Found In
Plasma membrane | Phospholipid bilayer with proteins | Outer boundary | Regulates what enters/exits the cell | All cells
Cytoplasm | Jelly-like fluid | Inside membrane | Suspends organelles, site of reactions | All cells
Nucleus | Double-membraned structure with DNA | Central (eukaryotes) | Contains genetic material, controls cell | Eukaryotes
Ribosomes | Small RNA-protein complexes | Cytoplasm or on ER | Protein synthesis | All cells
Mitochondria | Double-membraned organelle | Cytoplasm | Produces ATP through cellular respiration | Eukaryotes
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) | Network of membranes (rough has ribosomes) | Near nucleus | Synthesizes proteins (rough) or lipids (smooth) | Eukaryotes
Golgi apparatus | Stack of membrane-bound sacs | Cytoplasm | Modifies and ships proteins and lipids | Eukaryotes
Lysosomes | Membrane-bound vesicles with enzymes | Cytoplasm | Breaks down waste and debris | Mostly animal cells
Chloroplasts | Double-membraned organelles with chlorophyll | Cytoplasm (plants, algae) | Conduct photosynthesis | Plant cells, algae
Cell wall | Rigid structure outside membrane | Outside membrane | Provides structure and protection | Plants, fungi, some prokaryotes
Vacuole | Membrane-bound sac | Cytoplasm | Storage and pressure maintenance | Large in plants, small in animals
Centrioles | Microtubule structures | Near nucleus (animals) | Organize spindle fibers during cell division | Animal cells
Flagella/Cilia | Hair-like structures | External or cell surface | Movement or fluid transport | Some prokaryotes and eukaryotes
How Do Cells Move?
While many cells are stationary, others are motile, meaning they can move, either as whole cells traveling through their environment or by moving substances across their surfaces. The ability to move is essential for functions such as reproduction, immune defense, and capturing food. Cells move using specialized structures or mechanisms adapted to their environment and role.
Mechanisms include:
Flagella : Long whip-like tails (e.g., sperm cells, bacteria)
Cilia : Short hair-like structures that beat rhythmically (e.g., respiratory tract cells)
Amoeboid movement : Cytoplasmic streaming using pseudopodia (e.g., amoebas, white blood cells)
How Do Cells Reproduce?
Reproduction is a defining characteristic of life. Cells reproduce to grow, repair tissues, and perpetuate life. Different organisms and cell types use different modes of division, but all involve the transmission of genetic material to daughter cells. Understanding how cells divide helps explain everything from tissue growth to genetic inheritance.
Cells reproduce in several ways:
Binary fission : Simple division in prokaryotes
Mitosis : Eukaryotic asexual reproduction producing identical cells
Meiosis : Specialized cell division to produce gametes (sex cells) with half the chromosome number
What Do Cells Do? Cell Functions
Cells perform a wide range of tasks. These functions vary depending on the cell’s type and environment, but all cells carry out essential processes such as using energy, maintaining internal balance, synthesizing molecules, and responding to signals. The specialized roles of cells allow multicellular organisms to function as integrated systems.
Cells perform all basic life functions, including:
Metabolism (breaking down and building molecules)
Energy production (via respiration or photosynthesis)
Transport (moving materials internally and externally)
Growth and repair
Communication (via signaling molecules)
Reproduction
Defense and immunity (e.g., white blood cells)
Cell Theory
Cell theory is one of the foundational principles of biology. It describes the basic properties shared by all cells and explains their central role in life.
Development of the Theory
Robert Hooke (1665) was the first to use the term “cell” after observing cork under a microscope, although he was viewing dead cell walls.
Anton van Leeuwenhoek (1670s) improved the microscope and observed live single-celled organisms, including bacteria and protozoa, which he called “animalcules.”
Matthias Schleiden (1838) concluded that all plants are made of cells.
Theodor Schwann (1839) extended this conclusion to animals, stating that all living things are composed of cells.
Rudolf Virchow (1855) added the crucial third tenet of cell theory: Omnis cellula e cellula —”All cells arise from pre-existing cells.”
The Three Principles of Cell Theory
All living organisms are made up of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
All cells arise from pre-existing cells through cell division.
Modern Additions to the Theory Advancements in molecular biology and genetics have expanded the theory:
All cells contain genetic material in the form of DNA.
All cells share similar basic chemical composition and energy flow mechanisms.
The activity of an organism depends on the total activity of its cells.
Cell theory helps unify biology by showing that the diverse forms of life are fundamentally cellular in nature.
Origin of Cells
The origin of the first cells is a central question in evolutionary biology. Most scientists agree that modern cells evolved from simpler structures through a process known as abiogenesis.
Abiogenesis and the First Cells
Life likely began with self-replicating molecules, such as RNA, forming in the “primordial soup” of early Earth.
These molecules became enclosed in lipid membranes, forming protocells that could maintain internal conditions separate from the environment.
With time, these protocells developed metabolic processes and genetic machinery, evolving into the first true cells.
Prokaryotes Came First
The earliest fossil evidence of life dates back about 3.5–3.8 billion years and consists of prokaryotic cells.
These early cells likely used anaerobic respiration, as Earth’s atmosphere lacked oxygen.
Endosymbiotic Theory and Eukaryotes
The endosymbiotic theory , proposed by Lynn Margulis in the 1960s, suggests that eukaryotic cells arose when larger prokaryotic cells engulfed smaller ones.
The engulfed cells became organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts, forming a mutually beneficial relationship.
Evidence for Endosymbiosis Includes :
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA.
These organelles divide independently, similar to bacteria.
Their membranes and ribosomes resemble those of prokaryotes.
This evolutionary process underscores the shared ancestry of all life on Earth and explains how complex cellular structures came into existence.
Multicellularity and Cell Specialization
While some organisms consist of just a single cell, many forms of life—including humans—are multicellular. Multicellularity allows organisms to grow larger and perform complex functions through division of labor among specialized cells.
Cell Differentiation
In multicellular organisms, cells start as unspecialized stem cells and differentiate into specific cell types. This process is guided by gene expression and environmental signals. For example:
Muscle cells contract to enable movement.
Neurons transmit electrical signals.
Red blood cells transport oxygen.
Although all specialized cells in an organism contain the same DNA, they express only the genes relevant to their function.
Tissues, Organs, and Systems
Groups of specialized cells form tissues , such as epithelial or connective tissue. Tissues combine to make organs (like the heart or lungs), and organs work together in organ systems (such as the circulatory system). This hierarchical organization allows complex organisms to carry out diverse life processes efficiently.
Coordination and Cooperation
Multicellular organisms rely on intricate systems of communication between cells to maintain homeostasis, heal injuries, and coordinate growth and development. Specialization and cooperation are hallmarks of advanced life.
Cell Communication and Signaling
Cells constantly receive, interpret, and respond to signals from their environment and other cells. Communication is vital for growth, immune response, and coordination of activities in tissues and organs.
Types of Signals
Cells use chemical signals —such as hormones , neurotransmitters , and cytokines—to communicate. These signals may travel:
Locally , between nearby cells (e.g., in inflammation)
Over long distances , through the bloodstream (e.g., insulin)
Signal Reception and Transduction
Signals are detected by receptor proteins on the cell membrane or inside the cell. Once a receptor binds to a signal, it triggers a cascade of molecular events known as a signal transduction pathway, which often involves:
Second messengers (e.g., cyclic AMP)
Protein kinases and phosphatases
Gene activation or repression
Responses to Signals
Depending on the signal and the cell type, communication can result in:
Cell division
Gene expression
Movement
Secretion of substances
Programmed cell death (apoptosis)
Efficient signaling ensures that cells respond appropriately to both internal needs and external conditions.
Common Misconceptions About Cells
Many beginning biology students encounter confusion when learning about cells. Here are some common misconceptions—and the facts to correct them:
Misconception | Correction
All cells are the same size and shape. | Cells vary widely in size, shape, and function. A nerve cell looks very different from a blood cell or a bacterium.
All cells have a nucleus. | Only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus. Prokaryotic cells have DNA but no nuclear membrane.
Plant and animal cells have the same organelles. | Plant cells have chloroplasts, a large central vacuole , and a cell wall—structures not found in animal cells.
Viruses are cells. | Viruses are not cells. They lack membranes, cytoplasm, and independent metabolism.
The nucleus is the “brain” of the cell. | The nucleus stores genetic information and controls gene expression, but it doesn’t think or make decisions. It’s more like a library than a brain.
Mitochondria are only found in animal cells. | Mitochondria are present in both plant and animal cells—they’re needed for cellular respiration in both.
Cells always have organelles. | Prokaryotic cells do not have membrane-bound organelles, although they have functional structures like ribosomes.
FAQs About Cells
Q: When did the first cells appear on Earth? A: The first cells likely arose 3.5 to 3.8 billion years ago. Fossil evidence from ancient stromatolites suggests they were simple prokaryotes living in early oceans.
Q: Are viruses cells? A: No. Viruses are not made of cells and cannot reproduce independently, so they are not considered living cells.
Q: Do all cells have DNA? A: Yes. All known cells contain genetic material, typically DNA (or RNA in some viruses, which are not true cells).
Q: What is the largest cell? A: The ostrich egg is the largest known single cell.
Q: Can cells live on their own? A: Unicellular organisms like bacteria can. Most cells in multicellular organisms require cooperation to survive.
Q: Do plant and animal cells have the same parts? A: They share many features but differ; for example, only plant cells have chloroplasts and a rigid cell wall.
Glossary of Cell Biology Terms
Amoeboid movement – A type of cell movement involving the extension of the cytoplasm to form pseudopodia (“false feet”), as seen in amoebas and some white blood cells.
Binary fission – A form of asexual reproduction in prokaryotic cells where one cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
Cell – The smallest unit of life that can perform all life processes, including metabolism, growth, and reproduction.
Cell membrane (plasma membrane) – A semi-permeable phospholipid bilayer that surrounds the cytoplasm of a cell and controls the movement of substances in and out.
Cell theory – A foundational theory in biology stating that all living things are composed of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells.
Cell wall – A rigid outer layer found in plant, fungal, and many prokaryotic cells that provides structural support and protection.
Chloroplast – A green, double-membraned organelle in plant and algal cells that conducts photosynthesis using chlorophyll.
Cilia – Short, hair-like projections on the surface of some cells that move fluids or propel the cell.
Cytoplasm – The fluid interior of the cell that contains organelles and is the site of many metabolic reactions.
DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid) – The molecule that stores genetic information in all living cells (except some viruses, which use RNA).
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) – A network of membranes involved in protein and lipid synthesis; may be rough (with ribosomes) or smooth (without ribosomes).
Eukaryote – A cell that has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; includes animal, plant, fungal, and protist cells.
Flagellum (plural: flagella) – A long, whip-like structure that enables certain cells, such as sperm or bacteria, to swim.
Golgi apparatus – A stack of membrane-bound sacs that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for transport.
Lysosome – A membrane-bound organelle in animal cells that contains enzymes for breaking down waste materials and cellular debris.
Mitochondrion (plural: mitochondria) – The powerhouse of the cell; an organelle that generates ATP through cellular respiration.
Nucleus – A membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains DNA and controls cellular activities.
Organelle – A specialized structure within a cell that performs a specific function, often enclosed by a membrane.
Photosynthesis – The process by which chloroplasts in plant cells convert light energy, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose and oxygen.
Prokaryote – A simple cell without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; includes bacteria and archaea.
Ribosome – A small structure composed of RNA and proteins that is the site of protein synthesis.
Vacuole – A membrane-bound sac within cells used for storage of materials such as water, nutrients, or waste; large and central in plant cells.

Characteristics of Cells
All cells share the following characteristics:
Surrounded by a plasma membrane
Contain cytoplasm
Possess genetic material ( DNA or RNA )
Have ribosomes for protein synthesis
Capable of metabolism and homeostasis
Can reproduce (by division)
Respond to environmental stimuli
Types of Cells
There are two main types of cells:
Prokaryotic Cells No true nucleus (DNA floats in the cytoplasm) Lack membrane-bound organelles Found in bacteria and archaea
Eukaryotic Cells Contain a membrane-bound nucleus Possess various organelles (e.g., mitochondria, Golgi apparatus ) Found in animals, plants, fungi , and protists
Comparison of Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
Feature | Prokaryotic Cells | Eukaryotic Cells
Nucleus | No (nucleoid region) | Yes (membrane-bound nucleus)
Size | Small (0.1–5 µm) | Larger (10–100 µm)
Organelles | No membrane-bound organelles | Many membrane-bound organelles
DNA | Circular, in cytoplasm | Linear, inside the nucleus
Cell Division | Binary fission | Mitosis or meiosis
Examples | Bacteria, Archaea | Animals, plants, fungi, protists
Cellular Structure

Cells consist of a variety of internal and external structures that perform specialized functions necessary for survival and reproduction. These components vary depending on whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic, and whether it belongs to a plant, animal, fungus, or protist. Understanding each part’s structure, location, and function helps explain how cells operate as self-contained units of life.
Structure | Description | Location | Function | Found In
Plasma membrane | Phospholipid bilayer with proteins | Outer boundary | Regulates what enters/exits the cell | All cells
Cytoplasm | Jelly-like fluid | Inside membrane | Suspends organelles, site of reactions | All cells
Nucleus | Double-membraned structure with DNA | Central (eukaryotes) | Contains genetic material, controls cell | Eukaryotes
Ribosomes | Small RNA-protein complexes | Cytoplasm or on ER | Protein synthesis | All cells
Mitochondria | Double-membraned organelle | Cytoplasm | Produces ATP through cellular respiration | Eukaryotes
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) | Network of membranes (rough has ribosomes) | Near nucleus | Synthesizes proteins (rough) or lipids (smooth) | Eukaryotes
Golgi apparatus | Stack of membrane-bound sacs | Cytoplasm | Modifies and ships proteins and lipids | Eukaryotes
Lysosomes | Membrane-bound vesicles with enzymes | Cytoplasm | Breaks down waste and debris | Mostly animal cells
Chloroplasts | Double-membraned organelles with chlorophyll | Cytoplasm (plants, algae) | Conduct photosynthesis | Plant cells, algae
Cell wall | Rigid structure outside membrane | Outside membrane | Provides structure and protection | Plants, fungi, some prokaryotes
Vacuole | Membrane-bound sac | Cytoplasm | Storage and pressure maintenance | Large in plants, small in animals
Centrioles | Microtubule structures | Near nucleus (animals) | Organize spindle fibers during cell division | Animal cells
Flagella/Cilia | Hair-like structures | External or cell surface | Movement or fluid transport | Some prokaryotes and eukaryotes
How Do Cells Move?

While many cells are stationary, others are motile, meaning they can move, either as whole cells traveling through their environment or by moving substances across their surfaces. The ability to move is essential for functions such as reproduction, immune defense, and capturing food. Cells move using specialized structures or mechanisms adapted to their environment and role.
Mechanisms include:
Flagella : Long whip-like tails (e.g., sperm cells, bacteria)
Cilia : Short hair-like structures that beat rhythmically (e.g., respiratory tract cells)
Amoeboid movement : Cytoplasmic streaming using pseudopodia (e.g., amoebas, white blood cells)
How Do Cells Reproduce?

Reproduction is a defining characteristic of life. Cells reproduce to grow, repair tissues, and perpetuate life. Different organisms and cell types use different modes of division, but all involve the transmission of genetic material to daughter cells. Understanding how cells divide helps explain everything from tissue growth to genetic inheritance.
Cells reproduce in several ways:
Binary fission : Simple division in prokaryotes
Mitosis : Eukaryotic asexual reproduction producing identical cells
Meiosis : Specialized cell division to produce gametes (sex cells) with half the chromosome number
What Do Cells Do? Cell Functions

Cells perform a wide range of tasks. These functions vary depending on the cell’s type and environment, but all cells carry out essential processes such as using energy, maintaining internal balance, synthesizing molecules, and responding to signals. The specialized roles of cells allow multicellular organisms to function as integrated systems.
Cells perform all basic life functions, including:
Metabolism (breaking down and building molecules)
Energy production (via respiration or photosynthesis)
Transport (moving materials internally and externally)
Growth and repair
Communication (via signaling molecules)
Reproduction
Defense and immunity (e.g., white blood cells)
Cell Theory
Cell theory is one of the foundational principles of biology. It describes the basic properties shared by all cells and explains their central role in life.
Development of the Theory
Robert Hooke (1665) was the first to use the term “cell” after observing cork under a microscope, although he was viewing dead cell walls.
Anton van Leeuwenhoek (1670s) improved the microscope and observed live single-celled organisms, including bacteria and protozoa, which he called “animalcules.”
Matthias Schleiden (1838) concluded that all plants are made of cells.
Theodor Schwann (1839) extended this conclusion to animals, stating that all living things are composed of cells.
Rudolf Virchow (1855) added the crucial third tenet of cell theory: Omnis cellula e cellula —”All cells arise from pre-existing cells.”
The Three Principles of Cell Theory
All living organisms are made up of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
All cells arise from pre-existing cells through cell division.
Modern Additions to the Theory Advancements in molecular biology and genetics have expanded the theory:
All cells contain genetic material in the form of DNA.
All cells share similar basic chemical composition and energy flow mechanisms.
The activity of an organism depends on the total activity of its cells.
Cell theory helps unify biology by showing that the diverse forms of life are fundamentally cellular in nature.
Origin of Cells
The origin of the first cells is a central question in evolutionary biology. Most scientists agree that modern cells evolved from simpler structures through a process known as abiogenesis.
Abiogenesis and the First Cells
Life likely began with self-replicating molecules, such as RNA, forming in the “primordial soup” of early Earth.
These molecules became enclosed in lipid membranes, forming protocells that could maintain internal conditions separate from the environment.
With time, these protocells developed metabolic processes and genetic machinery, evolving into the first true cells.
Prokaryotes Came First
The earliest fossil evidence of life dates back about 3.5–3.8 billion years and consists of prokaryotic cells.
These early cells likely used anaerobic respiration, as Earth’s atmosphere lacked oxygen.
Endosymbiotic Theory and Eukaryotes
The endosymbiotic theory , proposed by Lynn Margulis in the 1960s, suggests that eukaryotic cells arose when larger prokaryotic cells engulfed smaller ones.
The engulfed cells became organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts, forming a mutually beneficial relationship.
Evidence for Endosymbiosis Includes :
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA.
These organelles divide independently, similar to bacteria.
Their membranes and ribosomes resemble those of prokaryotes.
This evolutionary process underscores the shared ancestry of all life on Earth and explains how complex cellular structures came into existence.
Multicellularity and Cell Specialization

While some organisms consist of just a single cell, many forms of life—including humans—are multicellular. Multicellularity allows organisms to grow larger and perform complex functions through division of labor among specialized cells.
Cell Differentiation
In multicellular organisms, cells start as unspecialized stem cells and differentiate into specific cell types. This process is guided by gene expression and environmental signals. For example:
Muscle cells contract to enable movement.
Neurons transmit electrical signals.
Red blood cells transport oxygen.
Although all specialized cells in an organism contain the same DNA, they express only the genes relevant to their function.
Tissues, Organs, and Systems

Groups of specialized cells form tissues , such as epithelial or connective tissue. Tissues combine to make organs (like the heart or lungs), and organs work together in organ systems (such as the circulatory system). This hierarchical organization allows complex organisms to carry out diverse life processes efficiently.
Coordination and Cooperation

Multicellular organisms rely on intricate systems of communication between cells to maintain homeostasis, heal injuries, and coordinate growth and development. Specialization and cooperation are hallmarks of advanced life.
Cell Communication and Signaling

Cells constantly receive, interpret, and respond to signals from their environment and other cells. Communication is vital for growth, immune response, and coordination of activities in tissues and organs.
Types of Signals
Cells use chemical signals —such as hormones , neurotransmitters , and cytokines—to communicate. These signals may travel:
Locally , between nearby cells (e.g., in inflammation)
Over long distances , through the bloodstream (e.g., insulin)
Signal Reception and Transduction

Signals are detected by receptor proteins on the cell membrane or inside the cell. Once a receptor binds to a signal, it triggers a cascade of molecular events known as a signal transduction pathway, which often involves:
Second messengers (e.g., cyclic AMP)
Protein kinases and phosphatases
Gene activation or repression
Responses to Signals
Depending on the signal and the cell type, communication can result in:
Cell division
Gene expression
Movement
Secretion of substances
Programmed cell death (apoptosis)
Efficient signaling ensures that cells respond appropriately to both internal needs and external conditions.
Common Misconceptions About Cells
Many beginning biology students encounter confusion when learning about cells. Here are some common misconceptions—and the facts to correct them:
Misconception | Correction
All cells are the same size and shape. | Cells vary widely in size, shape, and function. A nerve cell looks very different from a blood cell or a bacterium.
All cells have a nucleus. | Only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus. Prokaryotic cells have DNA but no nuclear membrane.
Plant and animal cells have the same organelles. | Plant cells have chloroplasts, a large central vacuole , and a cell wall—structures not found in animal cells.
Viruses are cells. | Viruses are not cells. They lack membranes, cytoplasm, and independent metabolism.
The nucleus is the “brain” of the cell. | The nucleus stores genetic information and controls gene expression, but it doesn’t think or make decisions. It’s more like a library than a brain.
Mitochondria are only found in animal cells. | Mitochondria are present in both plant and animal cells—they’re needed for cellular respiration in both.
Cells always have organelles. | Prokaryotic cells do not have membrane-bound organelles, although they have functional structures like ribosomes.
FAQs About Cells

Q: When did the first cells appear on Earth? A: The first cells likely arose 3.5 to 3.8 billion years ago. Fossil evidence from ancient stromatolites suggests they were simple prokaryotes living in early oceans.
Q: Are viruses cells? A: No. Viruses are not made of cells and cannot reproduce independently, so they are not considered living cells.
Q: Do all cells have DNA? A: Yes. All known cells contain genetic material, typically DNA (or RNA in some viruses, which are not true cells).
Q: What is the largest cell? A: The ostrich egg is the largest known single cell.
Q: Can cells live on their own? A: Unicellular organisms like bacteria can. Most cells in multicellular organisms require cooperation to survive.
Q: Do plant and animal cells have the same parts? A: They share many features but differ; for example, only plant cells have chloroplasts and a rigid cell wall.
Glossary of Cell Biology Terms
Amoeboid movement – A type of cell movement involving the extension of the cytoplasm to form pseudopodia (“false feet”), as seen in amoebas and some white blood cells.
Binary fission – A form of asexual reproduction in prokaryotic cells where one cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
Cell – The smallest unit of life that can perform all life processes, including metabolism, growth, and reproduction.
Cell membrane (plasma membrane) – A semi-permeable phospholipid bilayer that surrounds the cytoplasm of a cell and controls the movement of substances in and out.
Cell theory – A foundational theory in biology stating that all living things are composed of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells.
Cell wall – A rigid outer layer found in plant, fungal, and many prokaryotic cells that provides structural support and protection.
Chloroplast – A green, double-membraned organelle in plant and algal cells that conducts photosynthesis using chlorophyll.
Cilia – Short, hair-like projections on the surface of some cells that move fluids or propel the cell.
Cytoplasm – The fluid interior of the cell that contains organelles and is the site of many metabolic reactions.
DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid) – The molecule that stores genetic information in all living cells (except some viruses, which use RNA).
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) – A network of membranes involved in protein and lipid synthesis; may be rough (with ribosomes) or smooth (without ribosomes).
Eukaryote – A cell that has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; includes animal, plant, fungal, and protist cells.
Flagellum (plural: flagella) – A long, whip-like structure that enables certain cells, such as sperm or bacteria, to swim.
Golgi apparatus – A stack of membrane-bound sacs that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for transport.
Lysosome – A membrane-bound organelle in animal cells that contains enzymes for breaking down waste materials and cellular debris.
Mitochondrion (plural: mitochondria) – The powerhouse of the cell; an organelle that generates ATP through cellular respiration.
Nucleus – A membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains DNA and controls cellular activities.
Organelle – A specialized structure within a cell that performs a specific function, often enclosed by a membrane.
Photosynthesis – The process by which chloroplasts in plant cells convert light energy, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose and oxygen.
Prokaryote – A simple cell without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; includes bacteria and archaea.
Ribosome – A small structure composed of RNA and proteins that is the site of protein synthesis.
Vacuole – A membrane-bound sac within cells used for storage of materials such as water, nutrients, or waste; large and central in plant cells.

J.B. Hunt Transport Services’ third quarter slightly surpassed analysts’ lowered expectations following the company’s earnings warning issued in September.
J.B. Hunt ( NASDAQ: JBHT ) reported third-quarter revenue of $3.68 billion Thursday after the market closed. The result was ahead of a $3.59 billion consensus estimate. Earnings per share of $1.82 were 1 cent higher than analysts’ revised expectations. (A higher tax rate was a 4-cent EPS headwind in the quarter, partially offset by a 2-cent decline in net interest expense.)
The result was slightly better than its September update calling for a 5% to 10% sequential decline in EPS, implying $1.77 at the midpoint of the range. At the time, the company flagged near-term cost pressures—a sharp runup in diesel prices ($10 million), driver-related costs ($25 million) and elevated cargo claims ($10 million)—as headwinds. The actual impact in the quarter was over $50 million.
The third-quarter result marked a fifth straight quarter of year-over-year improvement to operating income and EPS. The company’s earnings turnaround started in the 2025 third quarter, well ahead of peers.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators
Intermodal revenue increased 20% y/y to $1.83 billion as loads were up 8% and revenue per load increased 11%. Higher fuel prices pushed revenue higher in the period. Excluding fuel, revenue per load was up 2% y/y. Volumes increased 18% y/y in the East and 1% on transcontinental lanes. A 3% decline in length of haul, due to a mix shift to the East, was a modest headwind to revenue per load.
The unit booked a 91.9% operating ratio (inverse of operating margin ), which was 15 basis points worse y/y. Higher costs (driver personnel, equipment and employee benefits) were a drag in the quarter.
The dedicated OR deteriorated 360 bps y/y to 91.5%. Revenue was up 11% y/y, almost entirely due to higher revenue per truck per week (inclusive of fuel). Revenue per truck was up just 3% excluding fuel. Average trailers in service increased 11% even though load counts grew just 3%. Higher driver costs, group medical claims, insurance premiums and new account startup costs were among the culprits.
The brokerage unit booked a second straight operating profit after 13 quarters in the red.
The company’s asset-light truckload unit swung to a $7-million operating profit after a modest second-quarter loss .
Shares of JBHT were down 2.4% in after-hours trading on Thursday. The stock fell 14% from its mid-September earnings update through the Thursday close.
J.B. Hunt will host a call at 5 p.m. EDT on Thursday to discuss third-quarter results.
Why it matters? J.B. Hunt’s quarterly results serve as a bellwether for the intermodal, trucking and logistics industries. The company’s third quarter was a modest slowdown after four quarters of strong recovery. However, some of the incremental costs that plagued the period were likely transitory in nature.

Lots of hardware news came out of the OCP Global Summit, which the Open Compute Project held this week in San Jose, California, and some of it is relevant to our HPC audience. Here are the highlights of the announcements.
AMD introduced Helion, a rack design based on OCP specs that it plans to bring to market with partners like Cisco, Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Wiwynn. AMD says it will work with the OEMs to outfit the 21-inch Helion racks (versus 19-inch for industry-standard racks) with its 6th Gen EPYC processors, as well as its new Instinct MI350P GPUs.
AMD Helion
AMD will give partners and customers the flexibility to tailor CPU and GPU configurations, including liquid- and air-cooled versions. The company plans to begin shipping Helion by next month.
Not to be outdone, Intel shared more technical details on its upcoming D-Series GPU. Codenamed Crescent Island, the GPU is built on Intel’s Xe3P architecture and combines up to 480GB of LPDDR5X memory, 1.5TB/s of memory bandwidth, and 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute, all within a 350-watt TDP.
The D-Series GPU, which is now sampling with customers, is designed to run the latest large language models and provide the memory bandwidth needed to manage the long context windows and concurrent demands of AI inference. Intel says the PCIe-based GPU will support up to 300 billion parameters on a single card, which will put it within range for LLMs with 1 trillion parameters in an eight card setup.
“Inference is becoming the defining AI workload, and enterprises need infrastructure that delivers the right performance at the right cost,” stated Anil Nanduri, vice president of AI Products and GTM for the Intel Data Center Group. “With Intel GPU D-series, we’re focused on making high-capacity inference practical to deploy and economical to scale.”
d-Matrix unveiled Matrix Squadron, a fleet of multi-rack systems offering megawatts of compute capability based on its Corsair XPUs, JetStream NICs, and its Aviator software. Squadron is available in several configurations, scaling up to 16 d-Matrix SquadRacks, which are single eight-server racks, providing a cluster with up to 1,024 d-Matrix Corsair XPUs.
d-Matrix developed Squadron in partnership with Arista , Broadcom , and Supermicro . Squadron has already been deployed by d-Matrix in its Arizona data center for internal research and development, and is now shipping to priority customers for deployment in their own data centers.
d-Matrix Squadron
“With Squadron shipping, and our Corsair servers and SquadRacks now generally available, the wait is over,” d-Matrix founder and CEO Sid Sheth stated. “Customers now have access to the world’s most efficient data center scale inference infrastructure available for building and ramping their ultra-low-latency AI applications.”
You can never have enough memory. In today’s age of massive KV caches, that saying has never been more true. With that in mind, Marvell Technology announced the second-generation updates to its Marvell Structera CXL memory expanders at OCP Global Summit.
The new Structera X 3406 supports up to 18 DDR4 RDIMM slots supporting 9TB of memory while the Structera X 3506 supports up to 12 DDR5 RDIMM slots supporting 6TB of memory in the CXL form factor.
“Marvell is the only provider with a complete end-to-end CXL portfolio spanning memory expansion (Structera X), near-memory acceleration (Structera A), and PFMA (Photonic Fabric Memory Appliance), pod-scale CXL memory-sharing appliance, giving customers a complete portfolio from direct-attach to disaggregated memory pooling,” stated Will Chu, executive vice president and general manager, Custom Cloud Solutions at Marvell. “We are delivering industry-leading CXL controllers, co-developed with leading hyperscalers to address the most demanding AI infrastructure requirements.”
Power is one of the big limiting factors in AI today, and OCP Global Summit featured various announcements on that front.
For staters, SolarEdge announced a solid-state transformer to support 800 Volt DC, the new standard that Nvidia is pushing to increase compute density in data centers. The company said that particular capability of the solid state transformer is currently running under load in its labs, with full power path and system-level validation expected soon.
(gguy/Shutterstock)
“AI infrastructure is forcing the industry to rethink how power moves from the grid all the way to the rack,” stated Shuki Nir, Chief Executive Officer of SolarEdge. “Our work on MVAC-to-800 VDC power architecture is about applying SolarEdge’s deep experience in DC power electronics and protection to that challenge, while working with Nvidia and the broader ecosystem to help establish the common interfaces and protection principles needed to deploy these architectures at scale.”
SSD maker KIOXIA America announced new direct liquid cooling (DLC) models to its CM9 Series enterprise SSD lineup. The new E3.S DLC models support new cold-plate-enabled servers, as well as traditional air-cooled environments.
KIOXIA CM9-DLC Series SSD is compliant with PCIe 5.0, NVMe 2.0, and NVMe-MI 1.2c specs, as well as the new OCP Datacenter NVMe SSD v2.5 spec. It features capacities up to 30.72 TB, and offers sequential performance up to 14.8 GB/s read and 11 GB/s write.
“The rise of AI infrastructure is driving a fundamental shift in data center design toward higher power densities and advanced cooling technologies,” stated Maulik Sompura, a senior staff director with the company. “The KIOXIA CM9-DLC Series addresses these evolving requirements by combining industry-leading enterprise SSD performance with direct liquid cooling support in the E3.S form factor.”
Kioxia-CM9-DLC can use direct liquid cooling
Texas Instruments (TI) also made some news with several announcements, including the first analog-to-digital converter (ADC) geared toward enabling 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution.
TI says existing monitoring solutions “often fail to detect the nanosecond-level power-rail glitches that cause costly, unplanned downtime in data centers.” But thanks to the combination of ultra-high-speed sampling with advanced on-chip digital signal, the ADC34DSO75 can detect and capture transient fault events in real time.
TI also announced the LMI800PS, which is the industry’s “first 800V isolated hot-swap controller.” The new offering replaces a “complex discrete solution requiring five integrated circuits with a single high-density package that delivers in-rush current and power path protection.”
Finally, TI unveiled a new bulk acoustic wave (BAW)-based oscillator that delivers what it claims is best-in-class jitter performance and power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR). The LMK6B can detect jitters of 9.6fs at 625MHz, which TI says will ensure reliable performance and preserve signal integrity for AI network workloads.
Also on the network front, Micas Networks announced three new 102.4 Tbps open Ethernet switching platforms based on Broadcom Tomahawk 6 technology. The new gear includes :
An 800G air-cooled switch delivering, delivering 102.4 Tbps of switching capacity across 128 800G ports;
A 1.6T liquid-cooled switch that provides 64 1.6T ports for high-density, liquid-cooled AI environments;
And a 1.6T co-packaged optics (CPO) switch based on Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6-Davisson architecture that’s designed to improve bandwidth density, power efficiency and link stability.
Eliyan’s new Nexus and Oscar NuLight chiplets
Voyant Photonics used OCP Global Summit to reveal its plans to develop a chip-scale optical circuit switching (OCS) engine for AI data center networks. Voyant is designing the OCS Engine to be a compact, reliable optical switching building block that can be integrated into next-generation data center switching platforms.
“Rather than developing a complete networking system, Voyant plans to provide its OCS technology as an engine that optical networking companies can incorporate into their own platforms,” the company says.
Voyant has already industrialized the underlying silicon photonic switching architecture to meet the demanding requirements of LiDAR for physical AI, said Clement Nouvel, CEO of Voyant Photonics. “We are now applying that foundation to one of the most important emerging challenges in AI infrastructure,” he stated.
Eliyan launched a pair of new photonic products at the show designed to help customers blow past the copper wall. The new products are the Nexus and Oscar NuLight chiplets , which Eliyan labeled “the world’s first 2D microVCSEL interconnect platform.”
Nexus is a 1.6T reverse gearbox, while Oscar serves as an electrical interface chip (EIC) that connects high-speed electrical interfaces to microVCSEL and photodiode optical arrays. “Together, they provide scalable building blocks for linking compute resources across large AI systems, providing the enhanced reach, low power, and high reliability that these systems demand,” the company says.
Nvidia and Cisco launched a new pluggable optics form factor, dubbed Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP), that the partners claim will help to scale AI factories by embracing optical networking technologies without overhauling their data center infrastructure.
“The first planned USFP-based transceivers will pack 16 full-duplex lanes in an octal small form factor (OSFP)-sized footprint supporting both switches and SuperNICs, with the ability to expand to 32 and more lanes in the future,” the companies say. “By doubling both the lane count and bandwidth per lane, USFP enables AI fabrics to connect more 1.6Tb/s endpoints without adding network tiers. Customers will be able to achieve 12.8Tb/s of overall capacity with USFP.”
Flex used the show to unveil new additions to its portfolio of data center racks dubbed Axiom AI Modules that adopt the latest in power and cooling technologies. These racks adopt 800 VDC power and advanced cooling distribution units (CDUs) to support the level of density that emerging AI workloads demands.
“The expanded portfolio is part of Flex’s Cloud and Power Infrastructure (CPI) segment, which Flex plans to separate into Axiom, an independent publicly traded company, in the first quarter of calendar 2027,” the company says.
