1962 Shasta Astrodome Camper With Turquoise Interior Is Deliciously Retro
10 photos
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Robin Burke
When it comes to vintage campers, it's hard to argue with options from Airstream and Winnebago. But Shasta is also a good option, especially if you're looking for something small and stylish. This 1962 Astrodome is one of those trailers.
If you're unfamiliar with Shasta, the company emerged in 1941. That's when industry pioneer Robert Gray opened a small factory in Los Angeles to provide housing for members of the US army. By 1972, Shasta was operating no fewer than nine facilities and had become one of America's largest trailer and motorhome manufacturers.
Shasta also changed ownership that year, being purchased by the W.R. Grace Company. It became part of Coachmen Industries in 1976 and eventually soldiered on until 2004. The brand was revived four years later, and it's still around. The Astrodome and Astroflyte are some of the company's most iconic campers from the 1960s.
Both are 16-foot travel trailers, and both feature the iconic rear wings and the front cab-over bunk. But the Astrodome got a few extra features, including a built-in toilet and a larger 30-gallon (114-liter) water tank (versus the Astroflyte's 16-gallon / 61-liter unit).
This Astrodome surfaced in Opelika, Alabama, and it's one of the finest I've seen in recent years. How so? Well, the trailer ended up with a loving owner in 2022 and received an extensive restoration since then. The camper was redone inside and out, with the overhaul having included a re-welding of the frame, a modern electrical system, LED lights, extra insulation, and lots of woodwork.
The windows were also replaced and released, while the entire plumbing system was redone. More importantly, the interior was refinished in a turquoise/white color scheme and fitted with vintage-inspired patterns, including fabric and wallpaper. The fridge/freezer, which isn't original, is also of the vintage variety. The layout is downright superb in my book.
The seller mentions that the camper still needs a bit of work to be perfect. While the fresh-water system has been redone, the trailer doesn't have a tank yet. It fitted with a two-gallon container on the counter, but it needs a replacement unit for the original 30-gallon tank.
Although it still looks pristine, the camper has been road-tested and used. The seller says it traveled from Virginia to Texas and then to Alabama, all while taking numerous other regional trips. The ad also mentions that the trailer's "sweet spot" is at around 60-65 mph (97-105 kph). "You'll also get a LOT of attention at campgrounds," the seller adds, which doesn't surprise me one bit.
The Shasta is for sale because it's too small for the owner's current needs, and you can take it home for $7,500 . While you can find cheaper examples out there, this Astrodome is not expensive given the extensive restoration. Where would you drive this tiny vintage motorhome?

Obrist, the Austrian engineering firm famous for ripping battery cells out of a Tesla Model 3 and bolting a gas engine into the frunk, is bankrupt. Three companies in the Obrist Group are insolvent with combined debts of about €31.8 million, or roughly $37 million.
The company spent over a decade pitching its “HyperHybrid” range extender as the smarter alternative to battery-electric cars. It never got a single production vehicle out of it.
Two closures, no rescue
The Feldkirch Regional Court in Vorarlberg opened bankruptcy proceedings at the end of September for Obrist Powertrain GmbH and Obrist Technologies GmbH, both based in Lustenau. The companies filed the petitions themselves, according to Austrian creditor protection group AKV.
Obrist Powertrain, the unit behind the HyperHybrid, owes about €18.85 million to 34 creditors. It was down to nine employees. Obrist Technologies, which held the group’s patents for methanol production and CO2 capture, owes about €6.08 million to 10 creditors and had no staff left at all.

A third company, Obrist DE, the group’s German sales and development arm in Lindau, is also insolvent with about €6.8 million in liabilities, according to ORF Vorarlberg .
There’s no restructuring plan. Both Austrian companies told the court that neither continuing nor restructuring was possible, and they agreed to shut down immediately.
The parent company, Obrist Engineering, isn’t part of the filings. It makes air-conditioning and thermal management parts and has about 30 employees.
Founder Frank Obrist blamed years of high development costs, failed talks with investors, and the crisis in Europe’s auto industry. AKV listed one more reason: European automakers shifting to fully electric vehicles.
The “worst Tesla ever”
We first covered Obrist in early 2020, when it unveiled its Model 3-based “Mark II.” The company shrank the battery pack to 17.3 kWh, stuck a 40 kW two-cylinder gas generator in the frunk, and claimed 1,000 km (621 miles) of total range. We called it the worst Tesla ever .
At the time, Obrist claimed it had already licensed the powertrain to an unnamed “international partner” and that production cars with the system would arrive by 2023. It also claimed the system would cost about €4,500 at volume and could cut the price of a Model 3 by more than half.
That partner was never named. No car ever shipped. We kept seeing these guys at car shows across Europe, but they never seemed to have more than demos.
In 2022, Obrist came back with a Model Y prototype running on synthetic methanol it branded “aFuel.” The pitch evolved from cheap hybrids to “climate-positive” driving: the company claimed the car removed 24 grams of CO2 from the atmosphere per kilometer because part of the captured carbon used to make the fuel would be buried underground.
And the claims kept growing. In 2024, Obrist announced an alliance with an Abu Dhabi-based fund and said an investment “in the double-digit billion-euro range” was secured for methanol plants in Namibia, Egypt, Thailand, and the US. It then pitched “gigaplants” costing $18.6 billion each, claiming the world would need 2,700 of them, roughly $50 trillion, to replace fossil fuels.
Lobbying for the engine
Obrist also spent years lobbying Brussels to reconsider the EU’s 2035 ban on new combustion cars. In late 2024, it argued that a HyperHybrid would emit 85% less CO2 than a comparable battery-electric car and called the technology a potential “lifeline for the European automotive industry.”
The EU has already bent on combustion more than once, from the e-fuels exemption Germany secured in 2023 to the Commission’s proposal late last year to soften the 2035 target. Policy moved in Obrist’s direction. It didn’t help.

American Electric Power (AEP), which said in July that it had secured about 13 GW of gas turbines for deployment through 2031, this week announced plans for a $4 billion, 702-MW Bloom Energy fuel cell plant in Wyoming to supply Google and purchased 190 MW of Mainspring Energy linear generators under an agreement for up to 1.6 GW through 2034.
Combined, the two announcements represent 892 MW of planned generation and purchased equipment, and pose the potential to reach approximately 2.3 GW if AEP buys the full amount available under the Mainspring agreement.
AEP said on Oct. 14 that Google will buy the Wyoming plant’s output under a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) from Cheyenne Fuel Cell LLC. AEP owns and controls about 92% of the company, and funds advised by Basalt Infrastructure Partners own nearly 8%.
The Wyoming plant alone is about seven times the size of AEP’s previous fuel cell deployment. AEP’s Ohio utility signed contracts in 2025 for about 98 MW of fuel cell service to supply two Central Ohio data centers that Amazon Web Services and Cologix operate, as AEP said in June 2025 . Still, the nearly 900 MW of planned generation and purchased equipment announced this week equals less than 3% of the roughly 33,000 MW of owned and contracted generating capacity that AEP reports.
A 702-MW Wyoming Bloom Fuel Cell Plant
AEP said it and its partners plan to start construction of the Wyoming fuel cell facility in 2026, and the plant is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2028. The company said Bloom Energy’s technology “can be deployed rapidly and provide reliable, on-demand power to meet the needs of large-load customers.” It also noted that the technology “generates electricity without combustion of natural gas,” and that the project includes plans to integrate carbon capture technology to deliver what AEP described as “reliable, near-zero-emissions power.”
The plant’s Cheyenne location and 20-year term echo an offtake AEP disclosed in January . In that filing, an unregulated AEP subsidiary entered into an unconditional agreement to purchase “a substantial portion of its option for solid oxide fuel cells” for about $2.65 billion. The subsidiary also signed a 20-year agreement with an unnamed “high investment grade third party customer” for all of the facility’s output. The January filing said that in November 2024 an AEP subsidiary had agreed to buy 100 MW of solid oxide fuel cells, with an option for 900 MW more. That month, Bloom announced a supply agreement with AEP for up to 1 GW and an initial 100-MW order.
In its Oct. 14 announcement, AEP noted the Wyoming project follows agreements, effective Sept. 30, under which another utility holding company, Black Hills Corp., will serve Google’s planned Cheyenne data center through 2048. Black Hills expects to serve the development through a 2.7-GW resource portfolio, including reserves, comprising up to 590 MW of grid-connected service and approximately 2.1 GW of third-party contracted resources managed through a private microgrid. The company plans to invest $1.8 billion in 564 MW of natural gas generation at its existing Cheyenne Prairie Generating Station through a nonregulated affiliate. Service is scheduled to begin in late 2027 and ramp to peak demand in 2030. Black Hills said the agreements are structured so that Google bears all costs of serving the data center.
The agreements support Google’s proposed $17 billion Project Tembo data center campus , which it is developing in partnership with Tallgrass Integrated Logistics Solutions, according to a Sept. 10 report by the Wyoming Tribune Eagle . The development was originally known as Project Jade, a partnership between Tallgrass and Crusoe Energy, before Crusoe withdrew in April 2026. A July 8 Laramie County memo identified Google, operating as Jupiter Star Holdings LLC, as the company pursuing revised plans for the campus at Switchgrass Industrial Park, south of Cheyenne.
The revised development comprises four data center buildings totaling approximately 3.08 million square feet. Tallgrass is developing an associated natural gas power hub, which Laramie County said was already under construction in July. At a Sept. 9 public meeting in Cheyenne, Ellen Zuckerman, Google’s head of energy regulatory work, said the campus would also use fuel cells combined with carbon capture and storage, according to the Wyoming Tribune Eagle . Neither AEP nor Black Hills has confirmed whether AEP’s 702-MW Bloom project is part of Black Hills’ 2.1-GW third-party resource portfolio.
“As power demand continues to grow, AEP is bringing together new technologies and strong partnerships to deliver reliable, innovative energy solutions quickly and at scale,” AEP Chairman, President and CEO Bill Fehrman said on Oct. 14. “This project demonstrates how we are creating new opportunities to meet evolving energy needs for customers both within and beyond our traditional service territory.”
The January filing said AEP expected the offtake conditions to be satisfied by the second quarter of 2026, and that if they were not, “AEP will be financially compensated for all capital and costs incurred.” The second-quarter 10-Q says the arrangement “remains subject to specified conditions” and that the deadline was extended in June by mutual agreement. “Should the revised conditions not be satisfied in December 2026, AEP will be entitled to additional consideration to account for the extended timeline,” the filing states.
During AEP’s July 30 earnings call, meanwhile, Fehrman said the amendment “modified some key protection terms so that AEP is adequately compensated for their requested timing accommodations.”
“Under the original December 2026 milestone, which remains intact, the hyperscaler has the ability to choose to deploy the fuel cells at an alternate location if the Cheyenne, Wyoming site does not advance. If the December 2026 milestone is not met or if there are additional requests to change the agreement terms, AEP retains financial protections for our shareholders,” Fehrman then added.
AEP’s October announcement identifies Google as the customer and confirms plans for the Cheyenne facility, although the company has not explicitly said whether all remaining offtake conditions have been satisfied.
190-MW of Mainspring Generators Set for Delivery by 2027
The Mainspring agreement , which the Menlo Park, California, company announced on Oct. 13, includes AEP’s purchase of an initial 190 MW for delivery beginning in 2027. Mainspring’s product page says the generator compresses air and fuel until “a uniform, non-combustion reaction occurs” that “pushes oscillators through copper coils 13 times per second to generate electricity.”
A recent datasheet lists 2.5-MW packages of ten 0.25-MW units that run on any blend of biogas, natural gas, hydrogen and propane. At that rating, the first tranche is equivalent to 76 packages.
Mainspring called the agreement “the largest procurement of linear generators to date.” It said the deal extends the company beyond the commercial, industrial and data center markets “into the investor-owned electric utility sector at gigawatt scale.”
The datasheet lists 46% electrical efficiency on an LHV basis, a heat rate of 8,233 Btu/kWh on an HHV basis and nitrogen oxide emissions below 1.5 ppm. Mainspring said it began commercial shipments in 2020 and has “hundreds of megawatts in advanced development and field operations.” AEP and Mainspring signed a 2022 memorandum of understanding to pilot the technology in Oklahoma.
“We continue to pursue new, innovative solutions to help meet the rapid growth in energy demand, support economic growth and deliver long-term value for our customers,” Fehrman said in Mainspring’s Oct. 13 release. “Mainspring’s linear generators can provide additional capacity quickly and efficiently, allowing us to better support growing energy needs.”
AEP’s Broader Business
AEP reported 69 GW of contracted load additions through 2030 during its second-quarter earnings call, up 6 GW from the previous quarter. On the July 30 call, Chief Financial Officer Trevor Mihalik said Texas accounts for 45 GW of that and Ohio for 12 GW, while Oklahoma, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, and Virginia account for the remaining 12 GW. The commitments are supported by a combination of executed electric service agreements and letters of agreement.
Asked whether more load could be signed before the third-quarter call, Mihalik said interconnection requests continue, though much of that demand is “limited by generation.” “This is where we’ve been very forward leaning in trying to secure those 13 [GW] to ensure that we can meet that potential load,” he said on July 30.
AEP said it secured 3 GW of gas-fired turbine capacity during the second quarter, bringing the total to about 13 GW, and is evaluating opportunities to obtain up to 10 GW more through 2035. “I would say that the 10 [GW] is an option for us. So we’re not committed to that, but we have the option to step into those slots,” Mihalik said. He said about half of the 13 GW was already in AEP’s $78 billion 2026–2030 capital plan.
AEP said it has line of sight to more than $10 billion of incremental investment, “including the fuel cell project in Wyoming, the Piketon transmission opportunity in Ohio, and incremental generation in AEP’s footprint.” These opportunities were outside the $78 billion base capital plan as of July. AEP has not said whether the Mainspring units fall in that last category.
The Wyoming schedule may also depend on a federal tax credit deadline. Asked on the July 30 call whether the project would be ready for AEP’s base capital plan by the third-quarter update, Mihalik said AEP had made timing accommodations for the customer and was “adequately compensated for that adjustment.” “But again, what we’re really hopeful for is that, that project will advance. And I think timing is key on that just because those fuel cells need to be installed and ready to go by the end of 2028 to qualify for the investment tax credit,” Mihalik said. “And so I think likewise, we will see some positive movement, hopefully, by that third quarter call and then roll that into the 5-year plan.”
AEP will report third-quarter results and introduce its 2027–2031 capital plan on Oct. 28 . The Wyoming offtake’s December 2026 contractual milestone remains ahead. The first Mainspring deliveries are scheduled for 2027, and the Wyoming plant is expected to reach full operation by the end of 2028.

What if the Honda e Returned to the Car World as an Electric Pickup?
12 photos
Photo: Behance | Mahan Rasouli
The Honda e may no longer be a thing, as the Japanese company pulled the plug on it almost three years ago, but that hasn’t stopped a rendering artist from imagining it as a pickup.
That’s right, you did not really think that the automaker actually revived this nameplate, and instead of a hatchback, it decided to launch a workhorse, did you? Yeah, that would be a no. As for the pixel master behind this project, he is Mahan Rasouli, and he recently took to Behance to drop these digital illustrations.
A side-by-side comparison reveals the differences between the real Honda e and this rendered pickup. However, between us, there was no need for such a thing, because the changes are more than visible. After all, the workhorse has room for only two inside. It also has a significantly shorter roofline, which was cut behind the B-pillars, and these are now a lot thicker, as you can clearly see.
Further back, the workhorse project sports redesigned rear three-quarter panels, which may follow the styling of the ones on the real thing, but they were adapted to fit the vehicle’s new body style. The tailgate opens up into the cargo area, and the pixel artist says that this thing would have around 500 liters (cubic feet) of usable storage volume. It would also be 3.5 percent longer, 1.0 percent wider, and 2.6 percent taller compared to the real Honda e.
Photo: Behance | Mahan Rasouli Nothing else has changed, by the looks of it, as the front fascia carries over with no mods. This includes the round headlights, the closed-off grille, and the bumper. The front hood is also the same, and the side cameras instead of the traditional door mirrors also soldier on from the defunct electric hatchback . The shape of the taillights, the trim in the middle of the tailgate, and the rear bumper are also the same.
Even the wheels have been retained, though from what we can see, they are a tiny bit smaller on the rendered electric pickup, and they appear to have been shod in slightly thicker rubber. We should also mention the new wheel arch trim, which is black, for a more utilitarian look, and the fact that this machine has a slightly higher ground clearance compared to the EV hatch on which it builds.
And the interior is also the same , by the way, to no one’s surprise, save for the obvious two-seat layout. The dashboard panel consists of three main screens, including the infotainment system, the display in front of the passenger, and the digital gauge cluster behind the two-spoke, multi-function steering wheel. These are flanked by two more screens, which are directly tied to the side cameras that have replaced the traditional door mirrors.
Honda’s e was on the quite futuristic side of things, both inside and out, and to be honest, it did not look half bad. In fact, it was very cute overall, but that wasn’t enough to save it from the chopping block. The company pulled the plug on it in January 2024, blaming the decision on poor sales. Production started toward the end of 2020 at the Yorii factory in Saitama, Japan, and this model was a subcompact electric hatchback, or a supermini if you will.
Photo: Behance | Mahan Rasouli It featured a rear-motor and rear-wheel drive layout, and came with a pair of electric powertrain options, which were rated at 134 hp (136 ps/100 kW ) and 152 hp (154 ps/113 kW), both having 232 pound-feet (315 Nm) of torque. Honda said 0-62 mph (0 to 100 kph) took over 8 seconds, and a Sport driving mode was on deck to sharpen things up. The car could also be driven in the Single Pedal Control mode, and had a range of around 140 miles (220 km) with the 35.5 kWh lithium-ion battery pack fully charged.
The retro styling and the mix of design and functionality have granted it extra points, but the limited range and the high price were the last nails in its coffin. Before it drove off into the sunset, the 154 ps Honda e Advance version was listed on the company’s UK website from 37,395 pounds, and that’s $49,500 at today’s exchange rate. By comparison, the MINI Electric was offered from 32,550 GBP ($43,085), and the Fiat 500 EV from 28,195 ($37,325).
In case you forgot, Honda never sold the e in the United States of America, because it was considered that the small EV segment and the poor autonomy would not be suitable for our market. It was, however, marketed in Europe, and, as we already told you, it did not do too well for itself, so the brand ended up pulling the plug on it almost two years ago.
Do you miss the Honda e? And if you do, what’s your take on this rendered Honda e Pickup?

Forest Find 1969 GTO Was Flooded So Many Times It Could Be a Reef, Someone Still Paid $550 for It
17 photos
Photo: YouTube/1Trailer2Another
Every red-blooded gearhead harbors a recurring fever dream where a forgotten Detroit legend materializes behind a dilapidated country barn for the price of a mid-tier microwave oven. While collector car auctions routinely gavel pristine muscle into the six-figure stratosphere, the universe occasionally rewards the brave with a miracle. How does $550 sound for a genuine 1969 Pontiac GTO, bought with zero buyer's premium and not a single penny of tax?
Before you call Barrett-Jackson to reserve a prime Saturday afternoon slot, there is a slight catch involving chainsaws, swamp mud, and Mother Nature's ruthless grip. The frantic wrencher from the 1Trailer2Another YouTube channel rolled out of his garage at 6:30 AM toward a rural farm estate auction in Martinsville, Indiana, armed with bidder card number 85, a pickup truck, an empty trailer, a chainsaw, and boundless optimism.
Hiding behind a weathered outbuilding in a low-lying ravine sat the main attraction, looking like Luke Skywalker's X-wing fighter after 30 years at the bottom of a Dagobah swamp. Local greybeards mingling near the scrap piles whispered that the wooded hollow flooded regularly, submerging the Pontiac underwater multiple times across the decades. Buried to its axles in mulched leaves, the coupe was pinned tight against a mature tree.
Even through a thick coat of Indiana moss and flaking red oxide primer, the car's factory green metallic paint, front fender "GTO" crests, and a truck-load of memories remained defiant. Up front, the once-revolutionary Endura deformable bumper still cradled the vacuum-operated hideaway headlights. Above them, the iconic twin-scoop hood had rusted into crunchy lasagna, folding in half over a complete 400-cid Pontiac V8 with chrome valve covers.
Photo: YouTube/1Trailer2Another Beneath that open-element chrome air cleaner sat a four-barrel carburetor, power steering pump, and alternator, though decades of aquatic adventures had most surely seized the rotating assembly solid. Inside, white vinyl Strato bucket seats flanked a console-delete floor tunnel sporting a manual shifter that turned out to be a 5-speed swap rather than the factory 4-speed.
Out back, the trunk pan and rear frame rails had completely evaporated. This GTO is biodegradable to the point where iron turns into trees and pain-in-the-necks.
Loose-lipped skeptics at the auction claimed the forest relic lacked a Vehicle Identification Number, potentially reducing it to a worthless LeMans imposter. Refusing to trust parking-lot gossip, our host pried back the shattered driver-side windshield glass, scraped away decades of grime, and uncovered the magic "242" prefix stamped into the dash plaque.
Photo: YouTube/1Trailer2Another When the auctioneer opened bidding in the weeds, bidder 85 jumped in at $50. Despite one bystander predicting a $1,700 hammer price , the warning that the car had no title and required heavy extraction equipment scared off the faint of heart. After a brisk volley of $25 and $50 bids, the gavel fell at $550. Moments later, the late owner's brother stepped forward to explain that his sibling had parked the ailing Goat there years ago, always intending to fix it.
With the car sunk deeper than the patience of a bull elephant during rut, the buyer arranged to return in ten days with a borrowed skid steer, while the brother generously offered an Allis-Chalmers tractor to help drag the hulk to freedom. Even if the shell crumbles during extraction, that authentic 242 VIN tag and cowl data plate carry the intrinsic value of the seismic revolution the Pontiac GTO ignited across Detroit.
When John DeLorean and his engineering rebels slipped a 389-cid Pontiac V8 into the intermediate LeMans for 1964, nervous brass capped initial forecasts at 5,000 cars, only to watch buyers snap up 32,450 copies. Sales more than doubled to 75,352 units in 1965 before hitting an all-time peak of 96,946 in 1966. That watershed moment coincided with the level up of the performance package into a full-blown self-aware model series.
Photo: YouTube/1Trailer2Another That tidal wave of success was followed by 81,722 units sold in 1967 and 87,684 for the restyled 1968 Motor Trend Car of the Year. By 1969, however, the muscle car wars had turned into a knife fight inside a phone booth, and total GTO output cooled to 72,287 units as the budget-minded Mopars (Plymouth Road Runner, Dodge Coronet Super Bee) and corporate sibling Chevrolet Chevelle SS 396 stole the sales crown.
Having dropped the pillared coupe after 1967, Pontiac offered the 1969 GTO strictly as a two-door hardtop coupe and a two-door convertible, alongside the flamboyant new Judge sub-model. Every 1969 GTO packed a 400-cid Pontiac V8 built around a 4.12-inch bore and a 3.75-inch stroke.
The standard four-barrel motor carried a 10.75:1 compression ratio and a Rochester Quadrajet carburetor to deliver 350 hp at 5,000 rpm and 445 lb-ft of torque at 3,000 rpm. Frugal cruisers could specify a no-cost two-barrel economy variant (but why?!?!) with 8.6:1 compression, generating 265 hp at 4,600 rpm and 397 lb-ft at 2,400 rpm.
Photo: YouTube/1Trailer2Another Speed junkies craving heavier artillery stepped up to the 10.75:1 compression Ram Air (III), which inhaled through functional hood scoops to produce 366 hp at 5,100 rpm and 445 lb-ft at 3,600 rpm. At the pinnacle sat the Ram Air IV with round-port heads, aluminum intake, and 370 hp at 5,500 rpm. Buyers paired these V8s with a standard 3-speed manual, a wide-ratio or close-ratio 4-speed, or a Turbo Hydra-Matic.
Breaking down all 72,287 units reveals 64,851 hardtops, including 58,126 regular, everyday, normal GTOs, and 6,725 Judges, plus 7,436 convertibles (of which 108 were Judges). Hardtop buyers chose the 350-hp V8 54,776 times, with 32,744 automatics and 22,032 manuals, while 1,246 took the automatic-only 265-hp two-barrel.
Another 8,129 hardtops got the Ram Air III, with 6,143 manuals and 1,986 automatics, plus 700 Ram Air IVs split into 549 manuals and 151 automatics.
Photo: YouTube/1Trailer2Another Convertible production followed a similar pattern: 6,800 ragtops received the standard 350-hp 400 V8, split between 4,385 automatics and 2,415 manuals, alongside 215 automatic-only two-barrel cruisers. Another 362 convertibles featured the Ram Air III, divided into 249 manuals and 113 automatics, while just 59 carried the Ram Air IV, counting 45 manuals and 14 automatics. When new, a 1969 hardtop started at $3,156 before options pushed well-equipped stickers past $3,700.
Adding the $185 4-speed manual transmission, hideaway headlights, power steering, and decklid luggage rack turned that $3,700 sticker into a street brawler that period testers at Hot Rod and Car Life clocked from 0 to 60 mph in 6.2 seconds and through the quarter-mile in 14.6 seconds at 99.55 mph.
A strong 1969 Pontiac GTO in good driving condition hovers around 50 grand as a median value in today market. However, the featured pile of discombobulated scrap iron parts that should have been a GTO project probably before this millennium, but ended up as a highwater marker for seasonal floods, is nowhere near that status. Frankly, I’m wondering if the price offered by a boneyard would even pay for the gas the YouTuber burnt on the drive to the auction location.

freight visibility meant knowing where a given truck was, but the industry has only gotten more complex as it has digitized. On a recent episode of FreightWaves’ What the Truck?!? , host Malcolm Harris pressed Andrew Wimer, Associate General Manager, Transportation Management at Descartes , on how visibility metrics have evolved as shippers, carriers, and brokers demand a fuller picture of what’s happening with a load.
Wimer, who oversees the Descartes MacroPoint visibility platform, said the fundamentals haven’t gone away. “It’s always been ‘Where’s my truck?’ or ‘Where’s the load? Where’s the freight?’” Wimer said of visibility’s original mandate. “That’s still essential. Don’t get me wrong. You need to know where your freight is or where your truck is.”
But Wimer argued the industry’s reliance on electronic logging devices has created blind spots that go beyond simple location pings, and that closing those gaps means rethinking who gets a voice in the tracking process.
For years, Wimer said, the industry treated ELDs as the definitive answer to tracking, fraud prevention, and driver accountability. That approach, according to Wimer, sidelined the drivers themselves. “There’s a massive network of millions of drivers who are very good drivers, who are reliable drivers, and who are safe drivers, and when they’re removed from visibility, they don’t have the ability to help validate shipment status,” Wimer said.
Validation covers everything from confirming a delivery to speeding up paperwork. Drivers who stay engaged with a tracking app can flag when they’ve arrived at a dock, upload proof-of-delivery documents on the spot, or send updates that would otherwise require a phone call to dispatch. Removing them from the workflow, according to Wimer, meant losing that layer of real-time confirmation just as the industry leaned harder on ELDs as “the silver bullet” for tracking.
The fix, however, is not to abandon ELDs. According to Wimer, “We need to bring the drivers back into the equation. We need to leverage ELDs along with the app within the driver community so that we can have the most robust dataset possible and improve our time to cash.”
That philosophy is the foundation of Descartes MacroPoint ELD+: to run ELD and mobile app tracking on the same shipment simultaneously, rather than forcing brokers to choose one data source over another.
“We’re combining the two data sources together,” Wimer said. “We’re tracking the ELD, the truck, and the driver so that you can have continuity over the tracking session.”
The redundancy is the point. If a driver’s phone loses signal, or an ELD provider’s API goes down, the other data source keeps the shipment visible instead of leaving a broker or shipper with a blind spot in the timeline.
“If there’s a gap in connectivity or signal or for whatever reason there’s an issue with one of the devices, the other one’s still picking up data and fulfilling any gaps in visibility so you can provide your shippers with good customer service and meet your compliance metrics and scorecards,” Wimer said.
Under the hood, Descartes MacroPoint no longer picks a single best identifier to track on a shipment. It tracks all of them at once, on one session, and feeds it all back to the transportation management system . “We’re tracking them all on a single session,” Wimer said. “We’re sending it all back to the TMS.”
Beyond redundancy, Wimer said the dual data streams give brokers and carriers a new tool for spotting trouble. When a truck’s ELD and a driver’s phone stop telling the same story, that divergence itself is a signal.
“Truck and driver should be telling the same story, moving down the highway together,” Wimer said. “If they go separate ways or signals go different directions, that should set off an alert and an operational workflow to call and investigate.”
A mismatch doesn’t always mean fraud, but it’s worth a phone call.
“If something odd is going on, get after it before it’s too late,” Wimer said. He pointed to a broader pattern the industry has had to reckon with over the past year: bad actors spoofing location data on both ELDs and driver-facing apps. “There’s spoofing of both ELDs and of the mobile app across any platform,” Wimer said. “Having multiple signals to help validate fraud and give you more data to then go out and talk to carriers is very important.”
There’s one specific scam that brokers run into often: a carrier selling a team-driver service (with two drivers alternating behind the wheel to keep a truck moving around the clock) while actually running solo, a bait-and-switch that can show up as a single phone number covering a load that should have two. Wimer, who spent time on the brokerage side of the business before joining Descartes, said he’s seen it firsthand. Tracking multiple sources of data, he said, is an excellent way to catch issues like that as they occur.
Rolling out the new ELD+ feature, Wimer said, required no new lift from Descartes’ TMS partners or the brokers using them. Using Descartes Tai TMS as an example, Wimer explained that a broker’s existing driver information (including phone number, truck number, and trailer number) flows automatically into Descartes MacroPoint to kick off tracking, and the solution handles the rest internally.
“ELD plus just starts off the bat,” Wimer said. “There’s nothing extra a customer needs to do.”
That’s a deliberate design choice rooted in how Descartes manages its relationships with the TMS providers that feed MacroPoint driver data.
“We don’t want to add complexity to what a TMS has to send to MacroPoint to take advantage of additional features,” Wimer said. “We want to handle that within the application ourselves, so that customers don’t need the TMS to do anything additional to reap the value from it.”
The scale behind that promise, Wimer said, comes from roughly two decades of building out the MacroPoint driver network.
“We’ve been building a driver network for roughly two decades,” Wimer said. “We’re talking millions of unique drivers on the network, with their cell phones. They’re ready to track.”
On the ELD side, MacroPoint has spent nine years building out telematics integrations and now connects with more than 500 ELD and telematics providers globally. Wimer said that Descartes has worked to maintain the network carefully so tracking doesn’t break down over vendor disputes.
Asked what shippers, carriers, and brokers should do first if they suspect their visibility still has gaps, Wimer pointed to the data brokers put into their own systems at the moment of dispatch.
“The first thing would be ensuring that you are working with your brokers on the floor to get full driver information. That’s the biggest gap we see,” Wimer said.
Wimer said he recognized the temptation to cut corners on driver data firsthand, from his own time working as a broker under deadline pressure. That habit, multiplied across an industry, is what still undermines visibility tools no matter how many data sources feed them, Wimer said.
“Getting accurate and good driver information in your TMS is still the biggest hurdle that I see our customers have,” Wimer said. “It starts with a good phone number. It starts with a good truck number or trailer number in the TMS so that then we have something accurate to track against.”
